title: Cells
explain: A cell is a complete, independently runnable and deployable copy of the service, and cells never talk to each other. Each customer lives in exactly one cell and a thin router sends them there. If one cell breaks, only its customers feel it, like a watertight compartment in a ship.
model:
A **cell** is a full stack (app servers, data store, cache, queues) that serves a slice of customers and shares nothing with other cells. (Chinese mnemonic: 细胞各自独立, 互不访问.)

```
                 +--> [ Cell 1: app + db + cache + queue ]   customers 1..k
 client --> Router --> [ Cell 2: app + db + cache + queue ]   customers k..2k
                 +--> [ Cell N: app + db + cache + queue ]
```

Why it works:

- **Blast radius = 1/N.** A bad deploy, poison request or dead database hurts one cell.
- **Unit of capacity.** Cap each cell at a size you have load-tested; to grow, add cells instead of venturing into untested scale.
- **Unit of deployment.** Roll out cell by cell, small and internal cells first, and stop at the first sign of trouble.

Rules that keep it honest:

1. No cross-cell calls and **no shared state**. A shared database turns N cells back into one failure domain.
2. The routing table (customer -> cell) is simple, rarely changes, and is the most critical shared piece.
3. Moving a customer between cells is a migration ([rebalance](#/sd/f/rebalance)).

Compare with [sharding](#/sd/f/sharding): routing looks alike, but a shard is only data while a cell is the whole stack.

details.q: 20 identical cells, one goes down. How many customers are affected?
details.a: About 5 percent, since customers are spread evenly. That 1/N bound is the headline benefit, and it only holds if nothing is shared across cells.

Anything shared on the request path: one database behind all cells, one cache, or cell A calling cell B's API per request. A shared user-profile database means its failure or overload hits every cell and the blast radius is 100 percent again.

details.q: Why cap cell size and add cells instead of growing one big system?
details.a: Behaviour at a tested size is predictable, a cell failure is bounded, and you never discover scaling limits in production. Capacity planning becomes counting cells.

details.q: How do you roll out a change safely across cells?
details.a: Deploy to a small internal or canary cell, watch error rate and latency, then proceed in progressively larger waves while metrics stay healthy. Halt and roll back at the first regression. Only a bounded slice of customers ever sees a bad build.

details.q: What does the router look like and why is it dangerous?
details.a: A lookup from customer or tenant id to cell, kept small and cached. It sits in front of everything, so a bug or outage there is a global outage. Keep it simple, static, heavily tested and deployed more carefully than the cells.

details.q: What are the costs of cells?
details.a: More reserved capacity overall, since every cell carries its own headroom. Global features such as cross-customer queries or global uniqueness are hard. Cells drift in size and need rebalancing, and moving a customer is a data migration.

prompts.q: Define a cell, and give two benefits and two costs.
points: Complete independently deployable stack serving a subset of customers
No cross-cell calls, no shared state
Benefit: tested unit of capacity and deployment
Cost: duplicated capacity and overhead, hard global features, critical router, migrations

prompts.q: Walk through a cell-by-cell rollout and what you watch for.
points: Start with a canary or internal cell
Watch error rate and latency per cell
Halt and roll back that cell on regression

prompts.q: Someone proposes a shared database behind all cells for convenience. Respond.
points: Shared state makes the cells one failure domain
Blast radius goes back to 100 percent
Keep data per cell, replicate or look up cross-cell data asynchronously if needed
Contrast with sharding: a cell is the full stack
